newsitem.title: INDIA: India to elect president on July 14.
newsitem.headline: India to elect president on July 14.

text.p: India's electoral college will vote for the country's 11th president on July 14, the Election Commission said on Thursday.
The panel said candidates for the largely ceremonial post, currently held by President Shankar Dayal Sharma, could file their nominations until June 23. Counting is scheduled for July 17.
India's electoral college, comprising elected members of the federal parliament and state legislatures, votes for the president of the world's largest democracy every five years.
Under the Indian parliamentary system, the president is the titular head of state and has few real powers compared to the prime minister, who is the head of government.

But in a year of political turmoil following inconclusive general elections in 1996, Sharma has wielded critical authority that allowed him to decide who would form the next government and whether to call fresh general elections.
The Indian constitution charges the president with appointing the country's prime minister. Over the past 13 months, Sharma has appointed three, all heading minority governments.
The president also has the final say in proceedings to impeach Supreme Court judges and in appointing state governors.
Since constitutionally secular India became a republic in 1950, the presidency has been held by upper-caste Hindus, a Sikh and two Moslems.
Vice President Kocheril Raman Narayanan, a former diplomat, is in line to become India's first low-caste president.
Sharma, who belongs to the priestly Brahmin caste, was the nominee of the Congress party, India's oldest political group, which was in power 1992. His term expires on July 25.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral heads a 15-party centre-left coalition government that leans heavily on Congress for crucial parliamentary support. His predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, in April lost a vote of confidence that was triggered by Congress's decision to withdraw its backing.
Gujral's cabinet on Wednesday approved an ordinance to prevent "frivolous" candidatures for the presidency and vice presidency.

The measure stipulates that at least 100 members of the electoral college must support a presidential candidate, who must pay a 25,000-rupee ($698) security deposit to file a nomination. The deposit used to be 15,000 rupees.
So far the most prominent contender for Sharma's job has been former chief election commissioner T.N. Seshan, who shot to fame in 1991 as a tough-talking crusader for free and fair elections.
Sharma has not said whether he plans to run for a second term. Traditionally, the vice president is elevated to the presidency, but Narayanan has not announced his candidacy. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
